a2-modal-can.title: Ability: -(a)olmoq ("can")
a2-modal-can.explanation: To express ability, Uzbek inserts ol (from olmoq, "to take/manage") right after the verb stem, before the tense ending: bora olaman (I can go), bora olmayman (I cannot go, negative adds -ma- before the tense ending too).
a2-modal-can.fact: The same ol also gives the language its word for "to get/receive" -- ability in Uzbek is literally framed as being able to "take" or "manage" an action, not a separate standalone modal verb the way English "can" is.

dialogue.en: Do you know how to swim?

a2-modal-kerak.title: Obligation: kerak ("must/should")
a2-modal-kerak.explanation: Obligation is expressed with the standalone word kerak after a possessive-marked infinitive: men borishim kerak (I must go, literally "my going is necessary"), sen borishing kerak (you must go).
a2-modal-kerak.fact: Because kerak is a free word rather than a suffix, it can also stand completely alone as a one-word answer meaning "[it's] necessary" -- much like English "must" can, but unlike most of Uzbek's other grammar markers, which are suffixes glued to the verb.

dialogue.en: Do I have to work today?

a2-comparative.title: Comparative & Superlative
a2-comparative.explanation: The comparative adds -roq directly to an adjective: katta → kattaroq (bigger). The superlative simply places eng ("most") in front of the plain adjective: eng katta (the biggest) -- no separate ending needed for superlative.
a2-comparative.fact: Because -roq attaches to any adjective with no exceptions, Uzbek has no irregular comparatives at all -- there's no equivalent of English's good/better/best needing three separate words.

a2-imperative.title: Imperative
a2-imperative.explanation: An informal command is just the bare verb stem: bor! (go!). The formal/polite command adds -ing: boring! (please go!). Negative commands insert -ma right after the stem: borma! (don't go!), boring emas rather borma ni ng orqali - kelmang! (please don't come!, formal negative combines -ma and -ing: kel-ma-ng).
a2-imperative.fact: The formal negative imperative stacks BOTH markers onto one stem in a fixed order -- -ma before -ng, never the reverse (kelmang, never kelngma) -- one of the few places in Uzbek where suffix order is rigid rather than flexible.

dialogue.en: Sorry, of course I won't smoke.

a2-connectors.title: Connectors: chunki & shuning uchun
a2-connectors.explanation: Chunki ("because") introduces a reason after the main clause: Men uyda qoldim, chunki kasal edim (I stayed home because I was sick). Shuning uchun ("therefore/so") does the reverse, introducing a result after the reason: Kasal edim, shuning uchun uyda qoldim (I was sick, so I stayed home).
a2-connectors.fact: The two words let a speaker present the exact same two facts in either order -- reason-then-result or result-then-reason -- just by picking which connector goes in the middle, without changing either clause itself.

dialogue.native: Ishim ko'p edi, shuning uchun kela olmadim.
dialogue.en: I had a lot of work, so I couldn't come.

a2-present-continuous.title: Present Continuous: -(a)yap(ti)
a2-present-continuous.explanation: An action happening right now takes -yap (or -ayap after a consonant) plus a personal ending: yozayapman (I am writing), o'qiyapsan (you are reading), ishlayapti (he/she is working) -- distinct from the habitual/future -(a)di tense covered at A1.
a2-present-continuous.fact: Dropping the final -ti (yozayapman instead of the fuller yozayapti-man-like form) is so standard in everyday speech that the shorter form, not the technically fuller one, is what learners should treat as the default to imitate.

dialogue.en: What are you doing right now?

a2-intention.title: Intention: -moqchi
a2-intention.explanation: To say what someone intends or plans to do, Uzbek adds -moqchi to the verb stem, then the usual predicative "to be" ending: bormoqchiman (I intend/plan to go), bormoqchisan (you plan to go), bormoqchi (he/she plans to go).
a2-intention.fact: -moqchi is built from -moq, the same ending that names a verb in its dictionary/infinitive form (bormoq = "to go") -- intention in Uzbek is grammatically framed as being oriented toward the bare infinitive itself, plus a state-of-being ending on top of it.

dialogue.en: What do you plan to do on the weekend?
I plan to go to the mountains.
